description: Project structure, .gitignore, and environment variables done right.

screens.body:
A tidy project has folders with jobs. Anyone opening it should guess where things live.

src/ holds your code. Tests live in tests/ (or next to the code they test). package.json, README.md, and .gitignore sit at the root.

There are no laws here — but consistency is kindness. Pick a layout and stick with it across projects.

options: src/ holds the code, tests/ holds tests, docs live at the root
Everything goes in one folder called stuff
check.question: Where does application code usually live?

code.snippet:
my-app/
  src/
    app.js
  tests/
    app.test.js
  package.json
  .env
  .gitignore
  README.md

screens.heading: A tidy project layout
screens.keyPoint: Folders with jobs: src/, tests/, root files.

screens.body:
.gitignore lists files git should never track. It's a bouncer for your repo.

The two must-haves: node_modules/ (thousands of files, rebuilt with npm install) and .env (your secrets — never committed).

Also common: dist/ or build/ (generated output), .DS_Store (Mac junk), and *.log files.

check.question: Which two entries belong in almost every Node .gitignore?

screens.heading: .gitignore: what never gets committed
screens.keyPoint: .gitignore = the bouncer. node_modules and .env stay out.

screens.body:
package-lock.json is the one generated file you DO commit. It pins the exact version of every package.

Without it, two developers running npm install months apart can get different versions — and different bugs.

With it, everyone installs byte-identical dependencies. Commit the lockfile, ignore node_modules: that's the whole rule.

options: Everyone installs the exact same dependency versions
check.question: Why commit package-lock.json?

code.snippet:
$ git status
modified:   package-lock.json   # commit this
untracked:  node_modules/       # never commit this

screens.heading: The lockfile belongs in git
screens.keyPoint: Lockfile in git = identical installs for everyone.

screens.body:
Environment variables are settings that change per machine: which port to use, which database to connect to.

Node exposes them on process.env. By convention they're UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES.

The || fallback pattern is everywhere: use the env var if set, otherwise a sensible default for local development.

check.question: How do you read the PORT env var with a default of 3000?

code.snippet:
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
console.log("Listening on", port);

screens.heading: Environment variables
screens.keyPoint: process.env holds per-machine settings. || gives defaults.

screens.body:
Typing export API_KEY=... before every run gets old. A .env file holds those variables as KEY=value lines, loaded by a tiny package (usually dotenv).

Your code stays clean — process.env.API_KEY just works — and secrets live in one file.

The golden rule: .env is in .gitignore. It holds secrets, and secrets never get committed. Ever.

options: In a .gitignore'd .env file, loaded with dotenv
Hardcoded at the top of app.js
check.question: Where do local secrets like API keys belong?

screens.heading: .env files for secrets

screens.body:
Not everything in .env is a secret. PORT=3000 is config — harmless if seen. API keys and database passwords are secrets — dangerous if leaked.

The test: "If this leaked on GitHub, would I panic?" Panic = secret = .env only. No panic = config = can live in code or a committed .env.example.

A .env.example with fake values (API_KEY=your-key-here) shows teammates what they need without leaking anything real.

options: API keys and database passwords — leaking them causes real damage
check.question: Which of these is a secret that must never be committed?

code.snippet:
# .env.example (safe to commit — fake values only)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/myapp
API_KEY=your-key-here

screens.heading: Config vs secrets
screens.keyPoint: Leak test: panic = secret. .env.example documents without leaking.

screens.body:
Two files do your documenting for you. README.md explains: what this is, how to install it, how to run it.

And package.json scripts are executable documentation — npm run dev tells a newcomer exactly how to start coding.

A stranger should be able to clone, npm install, npm run dev, and be productive in five minutes. If they can't, the docs (or scripts) need work.

options: What it is, how to install it, how to run it
A list of every npm package ever
check.question: What should a README answer?

code.snippet:
$ git clone https://github.com/me/my-app.git
$ cd my-app && npm install
$ npm run dev   # and you're coding

screens.heading: README and scripts are documentation
screens.keyPoint: Clone → install → run dev. Five minutes to productive.
